newsitem.title: USA: Republicans pick "pit bull" to head FBI files panel.
newsitem.headline: Republicans pick "pit bull" to head FBI files panel.

text.p: House Republicans Friday selected vociferously partisan Representative Dan Burton of Indiana to head the panel in charge of investigating the improper acqusition of FBI files by the White House.
Burton acknowledged that he had been "a bit of a pit bull" as a member of the House Government Reform Committee but said he would stress fairness in his new role as chairman.

During investigations of the White House travel office firings, he had suggested that deputy White House counsel Vince Foster might have been murdered and his body moved to a park in Virginia, where it was discovered.

"I'll be as nonpartisan as possible," Burton told reporters. He had been next in line to head the panel following the retirement of chairman Bill Clinger of Pennsylvania, who had held hearings on the White House firing of travel office employees and on the FBI files.

Burton is one of four senior lawmakers elevated to chair committees to replace chairmen who resigned from the House. Selection of these committee heads and re-election of 13 others brought no surprises and only one intraparty fight.

On the Appropriations Committee, Bob Livingston of Louisiana fended off a challenge from Joseph McDade of Pennsylvania, who sought to reclaim the chair after acquittal on bribery and racketeering charges. Republican leaders, pleased with Livingston's work at the forefront of the budget battle in the last two years, decided to keep him at the helm.
As a consolation prize, McDade was given the title of vice chairman and will chair the energy and water subcommittee.

Less straightforward is the selection of a chairman and members of the Ethics Committee looking into allegations that Gingrich misused a tax-exempt foundation for political purposes. This decision was placed in the hands of House Majority Leader Dick Armey of Texas.

The Government Reform Committee was expected to be one of several to look into allegations of illegal contributions to President Clinton's campaign by individuals tied to the Lippo Group, an Indonesian company.
"Democrats and Republicans alike need to get the information and get to the bottom of it," Burton said. But he said Republicans did not want a lengthy investigation.

He also said he hoped to wrap up the FBI files hearing, although the previous chairman said he did not receive all the information he needed from the White House. "We need to get the documents, conclude the investigation, issue a final report," he said.

The returning chairmen include Bill Archer of Texas on the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee, John Kasich of Ohio on the Budget Committee and Ben Gilman of New York on the International Relations Committee.

The three other new chairmen are Bob Smith of Oregon replacing Pat Roberts of Kansas on Agriculture, Jim Talent of Missouri replacing Jan Meyers of Kansas on Small Business and James Sensenbrenner of Wisconsin replacing Bob Walker of Pennsylvania on Science.
